title: The call is the answer
hook: a man stops calling on God because no answer comes, and learns his calling was itself the answer (Masnavi 3.189ff)
carry: the wanting is the answer, arriving

segments.voice: Yesterday, the elephant in the dark house, and hands that each touched only part. Remembering where your hand is.

You text someone. Two blue ticks, and nothing. You text again the next day. Nothing. By the third try, a little voice says: why are you still doing this? They're not answering. Stop embarrassing yourself. Plenty of people feel that way about prayer, or meditation, or any practice that doesn't send back a receipt. You keep showing up, and the sky stays quiet. Rumi tells a story about a man who heard that same little voice, and listened to it.
screen: `TWO BLUE TICKS, AND NOTHING.` → `THE SKY STAYS QUIET.` → `THE CALL IS THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. A man is calling on God through the night: Allah, Allah, over and over, until his lips grow sweet with it. And the devil, in Rumi's telling, comes with a very reasonable question. All this calling, and where's the reply? Where's the here I am from God? Not one answer is coming back. How long will you keep this up? The man's heart breaks. He stops, lies down and falls asleep. And in a dream he sees Khidr, the mysterious guide of Islamic tradition. Why have you stopped calling on God? Khidr asks. Do you regret it? The man says: no answer ever came. I'm afraid I've been turned away from the door. And Khidr gives him God's reply. Your calling Allah is my here I am. Your longing, your pleading, your ache, those are my messengers to you. The very pull that made you call was me, drawing you. Beneath every O Lord of yours are many here I am's from me. The man thought his call went up and the answer should come down, like a text and its reply. Rumi says it's already the other way round. In his telling, the longing comes from the one being longed for. Rumi is talking about God, and not everyone listening prays. But the idea travels: sometimes the fact that you keep showing up is the thing you were waiting for. Your line: the wanting is the answer, arriving.
screen: `ALLAH, ALLAH, THROUGH THE NIGHT.` · `WHERE IS THE ANSWER?` · `YOUR CALL IS MY HERE I AM.` · then, large: `THE CALL IS THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Settle into this sit the way the man settled into his calling, with no result expected. If you pray, you can pray, and let it be enough that you're praying; if you don't, just sit, and let it be enough that you're sitting. When a voice asks what the point is, notice it, and keep going.
Khidr. The mysterious guide who appears to the man in a dream and tells him his very calling on God was already God's reply. Today's word.
Your line: the wanting is the answer, arriving. In Rumi's telling, the longing was never one-way. Day two hundred three.

howItsDone: People who pray, in many traditions, describe times when prayer feels unanswered; in Sufi teaching this story is read as a comfort for those times, saying the longing itself is a gift from God.

chat.says: In Rumi's story, what did Khidr tell the man who stopped calling on God?
options: That his calling was already God's reply, the very pull drawing him close.
That he'd been turned away, so he should try a different prayer instead.
That he hadn't called loudly enough yet for any answer to reach him.
chat.meaning: In Rumi's telling, Khidr says the man's calling is itself God's 'here I am'. The longing comes from the one being longed for.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the superlative 'one of the tenderest moments in the Masnavi', 'green-robed' for Khidr (also in the match game), 'stop and feel' (told the listener what to feel), and the narrator's own theological claim 'you couldn't miss someone who wasn't there' (now attributed to Rumi); the 'pilgrims still say it' claim removed from the original note; howItsDone no longer generalizes about Muslims.

Paraphrased from Nicholson: lips sweet with praise, the devil's challenge, the man seeing Khidr (Khadir) in a dream, 'that Allah of thine is My Labbayk', the longing as God's messenger, 'beneath every O Lord of thine is many a Here am I from Me'. Confirm each.
Khidr as 'green-robed guide': the name is linked to greenness; confirm the description is fair.
Labbayk is the pilgrim's cry during Hajj; confirm the note.
The hook uses 'two blue ticks' (a messaging read receipt). Confirm this reads naturally for the audience.
